speaker: gm
text:
The yard smells of wet grain, pigeons and river mud. Above the shut loft door, a small grey-coated clerk turns slowly from the sack hoist, a pigeon hunched on the beam above him. A scrawny boy in enormous black boots lobs gutter stones at the body. “Missed again. Cob’s got better aim than that, and Cob’s got one eye shut.” From the wall top, a sharp-faced girl in a shawl swears at him and the world in Common, then switches to a harsher dockside curse.

A woman in a rain cape steps away from the open gate, notebook in hand. “Sergeant Agnes Kell, investigator. The Captain’s called it suicide. I haven’t.” She glances at the open satchel and bent spectacles near your feet. A stone clangs off the hoist hook.

marks.note: Cob” is the boy’s name for the pigeon perched on the beam.
The Watch Captain has publicly called Wendell Prout’s hanging a suicide; Sergeant Kell says she disagrees.

speaker: player
text: Maren Holloway, Sergeant, the King's asked me to look in. Glad you haven't. (I turn to the boy, gently) Lad, put the stones down, please. He was somebody. Stay close though, I'll want to hear what you saw, and there's a copper in it.

speaker: gm
text:
Kell gives you a brief, measuring nod. “Maren Holloway. Noted. The King’s asked you to look in.”

Cob stops with a stone cocked in his fingers. “Cob don’t take copper to talk. Cob talks when Cob’s got something to say.” His eyes flick to Kell’s notebook, then back to you. “And Cob’s got nothing.”

The girl on the wall gives a sharp laugh. “Listen to him, taking wages for a flap of his gums. He’ll be rich by teatime.” Cob’s hand lowers, though the stone stays in it.

Kell turns to the open satchel and bent spectacles. “I’ll note the satchel and spectacles, investigator. The boy won’t talk to the watch.”

marks.note: You offered Cob a copper to talk, and she’s mocking him for taking it.

speaker: player
text: (I crouch by the satchel and the bent spectacles, not touching yet, and look them over carefully: where they lie, what's inside the satchel, how the spectacles are bent. I write it all down.)

speaker: gm
text:
The satchel lies open by the gate, its empty mouth turned toward the yard. There’s no paper inside. The spectacles are several feet away in the gutter, one arm bent sharply inward; drizzle beads on the lenses.

Kell watches as you take in the details, then makes a brief note of her own. “Satchel: empty. Spectacles: bent. Noted.” Her pencil pauses above the page. “Nothing else in the satchel, investigator.”

speaker: player
text: A clerk with an empty satchel. Someone's had his papers. (I go stand beneath the body and study it: the rope, the knot, his hands, his neck, his shoes, and whether there's anything he could have stood on to reach the hoist.)

speaker: gm
text:
Kell’s pencil pauses. “That’s a theory, investigator. I can’t arrest a theory.”

From beneath the body, you can see there is nothing to stand on: no stool, ladder or crate beneath the hoist. The rope runs over the beam and through a slot above the closed loft door; the clerk hangs well out of reach. The boy’s next stone strikes the hook with a clang, turning the body a little. “There. He’s spinning.”

The girl on the wall drums her heels against the bricks. Kell watches you study the body, notebook open but her pencil still.

speaker: player
text: Nothing to stand on, Sergeant. A man doesn't hang himself from out of reach. That rope runs inside, so whoever did this was in the loft. (I try the loft door.) Is this locked? And can we get him down, gently? I want to see his neck and his hands.

speaker: gm
text:
The loft door is shut and barred from the inside. Your hand finds no latch that will open it from here.

Kell looks from the rope disappearing through the slot to the body above. “The porters tried it with a hook-pole. The bar held.”

There’s no ladder in the swept yard. The rope is taut; the clerk hangs high above you, beyond reach. Kell’s gaze settles on the ladder-less wall, then on the body. “We can lower him from the loft. Or cut the rope above his head. Neither from here.”

speaker: player
text: (I look up at the girl on the wall and speak friendly, no watch-voice.) You've got the best seat in the yard. I'm Maren. Were you up there early this morning? Did you see anyone come or go from that loft, or by the granary?

speaker: gm
text:
The girl looks down at you, heels still against the wall. “Early? I’ve been here. Saw him jump from the loft door at midnight, wailing about his debts.”

Kell’s pencil stops. The drizzle has left the bricks dark, and the girl’s shawl is damp through at the shoulders. She keeps her closed fist tucked against her chest. “What? You want me to say it twice?”

speaker: player
text: (I write it down, then look up kindly.) Once is fine. Only, that door's barred from the inside, love, so he can't have jumped out of it and barred it after. And you'd not have stayed out here all night in this drizzle for a sad man. Somebody tell you to say that? (I nod at her fist.) What've you got there? Nobody's in trouble for keeping something safe.

speaker: dice
text: Insight check to see through Moll's story about the jump: 17 + 6 = 23 vs DC 13: success

speaker: gm
text:
The girl’s chin lifts as if she means to fight the question. Then her eyes flick to the barred loft door, and the story loses its footing.

Her fist opens. A silver crown glints in her palm.

“A gentleman paid me at first light to say I saw him jump.” She closes her fingers around the coin again. “There. You’ve got your answer. Don’t go making it Cob’s.”

Kell writes, pencil moving steadily. “Witness: a gentleman paid her at first light to report a jump. Coin: silver crown. Noted.”

Cob’s stones go still in his fist. From the wall, the girl watches the open gate.

marks.note: You challenged her story by pointing out the loft door was barred from inside and asking if someone had told her what to say. She admits she was paid to give the false account.

speaker: player
text: Thank you. That was brave, and you keep the crown. (I pull out my notebook.) What's your name? And tell me about this gentleman: what did he look like, how did he talk, which way did he go after?

speaker: gm
text:
The girl studies your notebook, then looks at you. Her fist loosens a little around the crown.

“Moll. Good coat, silver-topped cane, wheat-ear ring, and enough lavender water to choke a horse. His big friend had a bandaged hand and called him ‘Master Sallow.’ He went out through the gate.”

Kell’s pencil moves. “Witness: Moll describes a gentleman as ‘Master Sallow’; silver-topped cane, wheat-ear ring, accompanied by a man with a bandaged hand. He left by the gate. Noted.”

Moll keeps hold of the crown. Her eyes return to the gate.

speaker: player
text: (I turn to the boy and crouch so I'm his height.) Cob, is it? Nobody's making anything yours. But those are fine boots for a lad your size. Where'd they come from? And did you see Master Sallow and his big friend here this morning too?

speaker: dice
text: Persuasion check to ask Cob where his boots came from and whether he saw the gentleman and his companion this morning: 14 + 2 = 16 vs DC 15: success

speaker: gm
text:
Cob scowls up at you. “Found ’em. They’re Cob’s, and no, Cob didn’t see nobody this morning.” He stamps once; the left boot gives a faint crackle.

“Shut it, Cob.” Her gaze stays on the open gate. “You already got him talking once, and now he’s trying to keep you from making it about him.” Her mouth tightens. “He said they’re his. Leave it there.”

speaker: player
text: (I glance up at the clerk's feet, to see whether he's still got his shoes on, then back to Cob, quiet.) They're yours, Cob, I'll not take them. But your left boot crackles like there's paper in it. Would you let me read whatever it is? You can watch me the whole time, and you get it back if it's yours.

speaker: dice
text: Persuasion check to read what's crackling in Cob's left boot: 20 + 2 = 22 vs DC 12: success (natural 20!)

speaker: gm
text:
Cob watches you for a long moment, then scowls and holds out his left boot. “Look, then. And Cob’s having it straight back.”

The boot stays his; the lining gives way to your careful inspection. Inside, a folded page is sewn in with small, neat stitches. It lists grain wagons marked “lost to goblins,” each countersigned “J. Sallow, for the Royal Purveyor.” Beside each entry, in pencil, are weights recorded at the river warehouses two days later. At the foot, a note: “Not goblins. Who pays the hedge-folk?”

Kell reads over your shoulder. She goes very still. “I’d met him.” Her pencil rests against the page. “Three days ago, Prout came to me about false entries in the King’s rolls. I told him to take it to the palace. I should have listened.”

speaker: player
text: (I copy the page into my notebook line by line, then fold it and hand it back to Cob carefully.) You kept this safe, Cob, and that matters more than you know. Did Mister Prout give you these boots, or ask you to hold them? Nobody'll call it stealing. I just need to know when you last saw him alive.

speaker: dice
text: Persuasion check to find out whether Prout gave Cob the boots and when Cob last saw him alive: 6 + 2 = 8 vs DC 12: failure

speaker: gm
text:
Cob snatches the boot back and turns his shoulder to you. “Cob told you, they’re Cob’s. Quit poking at it.”

Moll drops from the wall and moves between you and Cob. Her eyes keep flicking toward the open gate. “Come on. Now.” Cob clutches the boot, stones still in his other fist. Kell’s pencil waits over her notebook. The clerk hangs above you, turning slightly in the damp air.

marks.note: You asked whether Prout gave Cob the boots and when Cob last saw him alive. Cob shuts down your questions about the boots.

speaker: player
text: (I step back, palms open.) All right. I'm done poking. Moll, you keep looking at that gate. Is the big man with the bandaged hand coming back? (To Kell, low) Sergeant, if these two leave, I don't want them going alone. Sallow paid for a lie; he'll not like that it's been unpaid.

speaker: gm
text:
Moll looks at you, then down at the crown in her fist. Her voice goes flat. “I don’t know. He left with Master Sallow.”

Cob goes white and grips the boot tighter. Kell quietly adds Moll’s answer to her notes. The pencil makes a small, dry scratch in the damp yard.

speaker: player
text: Sergeant, will you keep the children near you for now? (I walk the outside of the granary, looking for another way into the loft: a ground door, a stair, a window, fresh marks, and I check whether the yard's been swept clean of footprints.)

speaker: gm
text:
“I’ll keep them here.”

She stays with Cob and Moll while you walk the granary’s exterior. The yard has been swept bare, and the drizzle has left no useful trail. You find no other ground door, stair, or reachable window into the loft. From outside, the barred loft door remains the only apparent access.

speaker: player
text: Someone's swept this yard, Sergeant, in the rain, before the watch came. Who swept it, and who holds the keys to this granary? A building full of grain has to have a way in for the sacks.

speaker: gm
text:
Kell looks toward the yard doors. “The yard was swept for the Assembly. The porters did it yesterday.”

She taps her notebook once with the pencil. “The warden keeps the key. She’s at the palace, counting provisions. Her runner came back with ‘After the Assembly.’ The Purveyor’s under-purveyors have keys too.”

Behind you, the yard doors remain padlocked. Kell glances toward the hoist rope running up through the slot above the loft door. “The sacks come through those doors, investigator. The porters’ ladders are locked inside.”

marks.note: The Assembly has the yard swept bare; the porters did the work yesterday.
Mistress Ida Garner is the granary warden and keeps its key. She’s at the palace counting provisions for the Assembly.
The porters’ ladders are kept locked inside the granary; the porters use the big doors to move the sacks.

speaker: player
text: (Moll's dockside curse earlier sounded like cant. I drop beside her and murmur in Thieves' cant, too low for Kell.) Easy, sister. I'm no bluecoat. Is there a back way into that loft the porters don't talk about? And where does a man like Sallow go to ground?

speaker: dice
text: Deception check to get Moll to tell you a back way into the loft and where Sallow goes to ground: 20 + 0 = 20 vs DC 18: success (natural 20!)

speaker: gm
text:
Moll studies you, then leans close enough to murmur in Thieves’ cant. Kell remains by the yard doors with Cob, out of earshot.

“There’s a loose board behind the water butt. Cob sleeps up there.” Her eyes flick to the gate. “As for Sallow, I don’t know where he goes.”

She draws back, watching your face. “And don’t go telling Cob I said anything.”

marks.note: A covert way of speaking used by thieves and streetwise folk, meant to keep outsiders from understanding.
You asked Moll privately in Thieves’ cant, out of Kell and Cob’s earshot; she’s trusting you with something she doesn’t want Cob to hear.

speaker: player
text: (I nod, keep her secret, and wander round to the water butt as if I'm just pacing. I find the loose board and squeeze through, then climb up toward the loft, quietly, looking at everything on the way.)

speaker: dice
text: Stealth check to pull it off: 19 + 1 = 20 vs DC 13: success

speaker: gm
text:
You slip behind the water butt and ease the loose board aside. It gives just enough for you to squeeze through, leaving the yard behind without drawing Kell’s attention.

Inside, the passage is narrow and dusty. You climb past the stacked grain sacks and emerge into the tally loft. A smashed lantern lies near the desk; ink has spilled across the boards. In the dust, scuff marks run from the desk toward the loft door. The great ledger remains chained to the desk, its open pages crowded with entries. At the far end, the rope is tied to a cleat in a compact knot.

Behind the grain stacks, a nest of sacking shifts. Someone in the yard calls, muffled by the wall: “Maren?”

speaker: player
text: (I stop still, hand near my dagger but not drawing it, and speak softly toward the sacking.) I'm not here to hurt anyone. My name's Maren, the King sent me for Mister Prout. Whoever's there, you can come out slow. (Then, louder, toward the wall) I'm all right, Sergeant, I'm in the loft!

speaker: gm
text:
The sacking shifts. A scrawny boy crawls out, eyes fixed on your hand near the dagger. His gaze flicks to Moll, then the loft door.

“You said the King sent you.”

From below, Kell calls back, precise and calm. “Heard you. Stay where you are, investigator.”

Cob edges no closer. “You’re not telling the bluebottle I was here, are you?” His voice is quiet now. Moll watches him, her face gone still.
